Brutus, my Lord. Nor for yours neither. Y' haue vngently Brutus Stole from my bed: and yeſternight at Supper You ſodainly aroſe, and walk'd about, Muſing, and ſighing, with your armes a-croſſe: And when I ask'd you what the matter was, You ſtar'd vpon me, with vngentle lookes. I vrg'd you further, then you ſcratch'd your head, And too impatiently ſtampt with your foote: Yet I inſiſted, yet you anſwer'd not, But with an angry wafter of your hand Gaue ſigne for me to leaue you: So I did, Fearing to ſtrengthen that impatience Which ſeem'd too much inkindled; and withall, Hoping it was but an effect of Humor, Which ſometime hath his houre with euery man. It will not let you eate, nor talke, nor ſleepe; And could it worke ſo much vpon your ſhape. As it hath much preuayl'd on your Cond • tion, I ſhould not know you Brutus. Deare my Lord, Make me acquainted with your cauſe of greefe. Brutus is wiſe, and were he not in health, He would embrace the meanes to come by it. Is Brutus ſicke? And is it Phyſicall To walke vnbraced, and ſucke vp the humours Of the danke Morning? What, is Brutus ſicke? And will he ſteale out of his wholſome bed To dare the vile contagion of the Night? And tempt the Rhewmy, and vnpurged Ayre, To adde vnto hit ſickneſſe? No my Brutus, You haue ſome ſicke Offence within your minde, Which by the Right and Vertue of my place I ought to know of: And vpon my knees, I charme you, by my once commended Beauty, By all your vowes of Loue, and that great Vow Which did incorporate and make vs one, That you vnfold to me, your ſelfe; your halfe Why you are heauy: and what men to night Haue had reſort to you: for heere haue beene Some ſixe or ſeuen, who did hide their faces Euen from darkneſſe. I ſhould not neede, if you were gentle Brutus. Within tho Bond of Marriage, tell me Brutus, Is it excepted, I ſhould know no Secrets That appertaine to you? Am I your Selfe, But as it were in ſort, or limitation? To keepe with you at Meales, comfort your Bed, And talke to you ſometimes? Dwell I but in the Suburbs Of your good pleaſure? If it be no more, Portia is Brutus Harlot, not his Wife. If this were true, then ſhould I know this ſecret. I graunt I am a Woman; but withall, A Woman that Lord Brutus tooke to Wife: I graunt I am a Woman; but withall, A Woman well reputed: Cato 's Daughter. Thinke you, I am no ſtronger then my Sex Being ſo Father'd, and ſo Husbanded? Tell me your Counſels, I will not diſcloſe 'em: I haue made ſtrong proofe of my Conſtancie, Giuing my ſelfe a voluntary wound Heere, in the Thigh: Can I beare that with patience, And not my Husbands Secrets? I prythee Boy, run to the Senate-houſe, Stay not to anſwer me, but get thee gone. Why doeſt thou ſtay? I would haue had thee there and heere agen Ere I can tell thee what thou ſhould'ſt do there: O Conſtancie, be ſtrong vpon my ſide, Set a huge Mountaine 'tweene my Heart and Tongue: I haue a mans minde, but a womans might: How hard it is for women to keepe counſell. Art thou heere yet? Yes, bring me word Boy, if thy Lord look well, For he went ſickly forth: and take good note What Caeſar doth, what Sutors preſſe to him. Hearke Boy, what noyſe is that? Prythee liſten well: I heard a buſsling Rumor like a Fray, And the winde brings it from the Capitoll. Come hither Fellow, which way haſt thou bin? What is't a clocke? Is Caeſar yet gone to the Capitoll? Thou haſt ſome ſuite to Caeſar, haſt thou not? Why know'ſt thou any harme's intended to wards him? I muſt go in: Aye me! How weake a thing The heart of woman is? O Brutus, The Heauens ſpeede thee in thine enterprize. Sure the Boy heard me ▪ Brutus hath a ſuite That Caeſar will not grant. O, I grow faint: Run Lucius, and commend me to my Lord, Say I am merry; Come to me againe, And bring me word what he doth ſay to thee.
Vouchſafe good morrow from a feeble tongue. I am not ſicke, if Brutus haue in hand Any exploit worthy the name of Honor. By all the Gods that Romans bow before, I heere diſcard my ſickneſſe. Soule of Rome, Braue Sonne, deriu'd from Honourable Loines, Thou like an Exorciſt, haſt coniur'd vp My mortified Spirit. Now bid me runne, And I will ſtriue with things impoſſible, Yea get the better of them. What's to do? But are not ſome whole ▪ that we muſt make ſicke? Set on your foote, And with a heart new-fir'd, I follow you, To do I know not what: but it ſufficeth That Brutus leads me on.

Thus Brutus did my Maſter bid me kneele; Thus did Mark Antony bid me fall downe, And being proſtrate, thus he bad me ſay: Brutus is Noble, Wiſe, Valiant, and Honeſt; Caeſar was Mighty, Bold, Royall, and Louing: Say, I loue Brutus, and I honour him; Say, I fear'd Caeſar, honour'd him, and lou'd him. He lies to night within ſeuen Leagues of Rome. Sir, Octauius is already come to Rome. He and Lepidus are at Caeſars houſe. I heard him ſay, Brutus and Caſſius Are rid like Madmen through the Gates of Rome.
What mean you Caeſar ? Think you to walk forth? You ſhall not ſtirre out of your houſe to day.
Caeſar, all haile: Good morrow worthy Caeſar, I come to fetch you to the Senate houſe. Moſt mighty Caeſar let me know ſome cauſe, Leſt I be laught at when I tell them ſo. This Dreame is all amiſſe interpreted, It was a viſion, faire and fortunate: Your Statue ſpouting blood in many pipes, In which ſo many ſmiling Romans bath'd, Signifies, that from you great Rome ſhall ſucke Reuiuing blood, and that great men ſhall preſſe For Tinctures, Staines, Reliques, and Cogniſance. This by Calphurnia 's Dreame is ſignified. I haue, when you haue heard what I can ſay: And know it now, the Senate haue concluded To giue this day, a Crowne to mighty Caeſar. If you ſhall ſend them word you will not come, Their mindes may change. Beſides, it were a mocke Apt to be render'd, for ſome one to ſay, Breake vp the Senate, till another time: When Caeſars wife ſhall meete with better Dreames. If Caeſar hide himſelfe, ſhall they not whiſper Loe Caeſar is affraid? Pardon me Caeſar, for my deere deere loue To your proceeding, bids me tell you this: And reaſon to my loue is liable. Trebonius doth deſire you to ore-read (At your beſt leyſure) this his humble ſuite. Where is Metellus Cimber, let him go, And preſently preferre his ſuite to Caeſar.
Good morrow Caeſar. Sirra, giue place.
Haile Caeſar : Read this Scedule. O Caeſar, reade mine firſt: for mine's a ſuite That touches Caeſar neerer. Read it great Caeſar. Delay not Caeſar, read it inſtantly.
I wiſh your enterprize to day may thriue. Fare you well.
And Caſſius too. What, ſhall we forth?

I will heare Brutus ſpeake. Neuer, neuer: come, away, away: Wee'l burne his body in the holy place, And with the Brands fire the Traitors houſes. Take vp the body.
I will heare Caſſius, and compare their Reaſons, When ſeuerally we heare them rendred. Giue him a Statue with his Anceſtors. Peace, ſilence, Brutus ſpeakes. Poore ſoule, his eyes are red as fire with weeping. O Noble Caeſar ! We will be reueng'd: Reuenge About, ſeeke, burne, fire, kill, ſlay, Let not a Traitor liue. Wee'l heare him, wee'l follow him, wee'l dy with him. Whether are you going? Anſwer euery man directly. That matter is anſwered directly.
The Noble Brutus is aſcended: Silence. Let him be Caeſar. There's not a Nobler man in Rome then Antony. O wofull day! Where do you dwell? I, and truly, you were beſt. Your name ſir, truly. Teare him, tear him; Come Brands hoe, Firebrands: to Brutus, to Caſſius, burne all. Some to Decius Houſe, and ſome to Caska 's; ſome to Ligarius: Away, go.
None Brutus, none. Liue Brutus, liue, liue. Peace hoe, let vs heare him. The Will, the Will; we will heare Caeſars Will. The Will, the Teſtament. Come downe. Stand backe: roome, beare backe. Wee'l Mutiny. Peace hoe, heare Antony, moſt Noble Antony. Moſt true, the Will, let's ſtay and heare the Wil. Peace hoe
Bring him with Triumph home vnto his houſe. Wee'l bring him to his Houſe, With Showts and Clamors. Peace ho. If it be found ſo, ſome will deere abide it. O pitteous ſpectacle! O moſt bloody ſight! Peace there, heare the Noble Antony. What is your name? I, and breefely. As a Friend, or an Enemy? Teare him to peeces, hee's a Conſpirator.
Caeſars better parts, Shall be Crown'd in Brutus. Mark'd ye his words? he would not take y e Crown, Therefore 'tis certaine, he was not Ambitious. Now marke him, he begins againe to ſpeake. O Traitors, Villaines! Are you a married man, or a Batchellor? I, and wiſely. For your dwelling: breefely. Teare him for his bad verſes, teare him for his bad Verſes. It is no matter, his name's Cinna, plucke but his name out of his heart, and turne him going.
speeches.1: Stay ho, and let vs heare Mark Antony. This Caeſar was a Tyrant. Me thinkes there is much reaſon in his ſayings. Stand from the Hearſe, ſtand from the Body. Wee'l burne the houſe of Brutus.
speeches.3: Let him go vp into the publike Chaire, Wee'l heare him: Noble Antony go vp. He ſayes, for Brutus ſake He findes himſelfe beholding to vs all. Nay that's certaine: We are bleſt that Rome is rid of him. Ha's hee Maſters? I feare there will a worſe come in his place. You ſhall haue leaue. Away then, come, ſeeke the Conſpirators.
speeches.4: What does he ſay of Brutus? 'Twere beſt he ſpeake no harme of Brutus heere? Wee'l heare the Will, reade it Marke Antony. Read the Will, wee'l heare it Antony: You ſhall reade vs the Will, Caeſars Will. They were Traitors: Honourable men? A Ring, ſtand round.
speeches.2: Peace, let vs heare what Antony can ſay. If thou conſider rightly of the matter, Caeſar ha's had great wrong. They were Villaines, Murderers: the Will, read the Will. Deſcend. Roome for Antony, moſt Noble Antony. That's as much as to ſay, they are fooles that mar rie: you'l beare me a bang for that I feare: proceede di rectly.
Friends, Romans, Countrymen, lend me your ears: I come to bury Caeſar, not to praiſe him: The euill that men do, liues after them, The good is oft enterred with their bones, So let it be with Caeſar. The Noble Brutus, Hath told you Caeſar was Ambitious: If it were ſo, it was a greeuous Fault, And greeuouſly hath Caeſar anſwer'd it. Heere, vnder leaue of Brutus, and the reſt (For Brutus is an Honourable man, So are they all; all Honourable m • n) Come I to ſpeake in Caeſars Funerall. He was my Friend, faithfull, and iuſt to me; But Brutus ſayes; he was Ambitious, And Brutus is an Honourable man. He hath brought many Captiues home to Rome ▪ Whoſe Ranſomes, did the generall Coffers fill: Did this in Caeſar ſeeme Ambitious? When that the poore haue cry'de, Caeſar hath wept: Ambition ſhould be made of ſterner ſtuffe, Yet Brutus ſayes, he was Ambitious: And Brutus is an Honourable man. You all did ſee, that on the Lupercall, I thrice preſented him a Kingly Crowne, Which he did thrice refuſe. Was this Ambition? Yet Brutus ſayes, he was Ambitious: And ſure he is an Honourable man. I ſpeake not to diſprooue what Brutus ſpoke, But heere I am, to ſpeake what I do know; You all did loue him once, not without cauſe, What cauſe with-holds you then, to mourne for him? O Iudgement! thou are fled to brutiſh Beaſts, And Men haue loſt their Reaſon. Beare with me, My heart is in the Coffin there with Caeſar, And I muſt pawſe, till it come backe to me. In your bad ſtrokes Brutus, you giue good words Witneſſe the hole you made in Caeſars heart, Crying long liue, Haile Caeſar.
Moſt Noble Caeſar, wee'l reuenge his death.
Plucke downe Formes, Windowes, any thing.

Your Brother too muſt dye: conſent you Lepidus ? Pricke him downe Antony. Or heere, or at the Capitoll. So you thought him, And tooke his voyce who ſhould be prickt to dye In our blacke Sentence and Proſcription. You may do your will: But hee's a tried, and valiant Souldier. Let vs do ſo: for we are at the ſtake, And bayed about with many Enemies, And ſome that ſmile haue in their hearts I feare Millions of Miſcheefes. Now Antony, our hopes are anſwered, You ſaid the Enemy would not come downe, But keepe the Hilles and vpper Regions: It proues not ſo: their battailes are at hand, They meane to warne vs at Philippi heere: Anſwering before we do demand of them. Vpon the right hand I, keepe thou the left. I do not croſſe you: but I will do ſo. Mark Antony, ſhall we giue ſigne of Battaile? Not that we loue words better, as you do. Come, come, the cauſe. If arguing make vs ſwet, The proofe of it will turne to redder drops: Looke, I draw a Sword againſt Conſpirators, When thinke you that the Sword goes vp againe? Neuer till Caeſars three and thirtie wounds Be well aueng'd; or till another Caeſar Haue added ſlaughter to the Sword of Traitors. So I hope: I was not borne to dye on Brutus Sword. Come Antony : away: Defiance Traitors, hurle we in your teeth. If you dare fight to day, come to the Field; If not, when you haue ſtomackes. What man is that? All that ſeru'd Brutus, I will entertaine them. Fellow, wilt thou beſtow thy time with me? Do ſo, good Meſſala. According to his Vertue, let vs vſe him Withall Reſpect, and Rites of Buriall. Within my Tent his bones to night ſhall ly ▪ Moſt like a Souldier ordered Honourably: So call the Field to reſt, and let's away, To part the glories of this happy day.
I do conſent. Vpon condition Publius ſhall not liue, Who is your Siſters ſonne, Marke Antony. What? ſhall I finde you heere?
Giue the word ho, and Stand. He is at hand, and Pindarus is come To do you ſalutation from his Maſter. With courteſie, and with reſpect enough, But not with ſuch familiar inſtances, Nor with ſuch free and friendly Conference As he hath vs'd of old. They meane this night in Sardis to be quarter'd: The greater part, the Horſe in generall Are come with Caſſius. You ſhall not come to them. So Brutus ſhould be found. I thank thee Brutus That thou haſt prou'd Lucillius ſaying true,
I do not doubt But that my Noble Maſter will appeare Such as he is, full of regard, and Honour. So, I am free, Yet would not ſo haue beene Durſt I haue done my will. O Caſſius, Farre from this Country Pindarus ſhall run, Where neuer Roman ſhall take note of him.
Let me go in to ſee the Generals, There is ſome grudge betweene 'em, 'tis not meete They be alone. Nothing but death ſhall ſtay me. For ſhame you Generals; what do you meane? Loue, and be Friends, as two ſuch men ſhould bee, For I haue ſeene more yeeres I'me ſure then yee.
My ſelfe haue Letters of the ſelfe-ſame Tenure. That by proſcription, and billes of Outlarie, Octauius, Antony, and Lepidus, Haue put to death, an hundred Senators.
Cicero is dead, and by that order of proſcription Had you your Letters from your wife, my Lord? Nor nothing in your Letters writ of her? That me thinkes is ſtrange. No my Lord. Then like a Roman, beare the truth I tell, For certaine ſhe is dead, and by ſtrange manner. Euen ſo great men, great loſſes ſhold indure. What ſayes my Generall? Beleeue not ſo. It is but change, Titinius : for Octauius Is ouerthrowne by Noble Brutus power, As Caſſius Legions are by Antony. Where did you leaue him. Is not that he that lyes vpon the ground? Is not that hee? Miſtruſt of good ſucceſſe hath done this deed. O hatefull Error, Melancholies Childe: Why do'ſt thou ſhew to the apt thoughts of men ▪ The things that are not? O Error ſoone conceyu'd, Thou neuer com'ſt vnto a happy byrth, But kil'ſt the Mother that engendred thee. Seeke him Titinius, whilſt I go to meet The Noble Brutus, thruſting this report Into his eares; I may ſay thruſting it: For piercing Steele, and Darts inuenomed, Shall be as welcome to the eares of Brutus, As tydings of this ſight. Loe yonder, and Titinius mourning it. My Maſters man. Strato, where is thy Maſter? How dyed my Maſter Strato ? Octauius, then take him to follow thee, That did the lateſt ſeruice to my Maſter.
Cals my Lord? So pleaſe you, we will ſtand, And watch your pleaſure. My Lord. No my Lord, I ſaw nothing.
Thy euill Spirit Brutus ? To tell thee thou ſhalt ſee me at Philippi. I, at Philippi.
Did we my Lord? It ſhall be done my Lord.
Prepare you Generals, The Enemy comes on in gallant ſhew: Their bloody ſigne of Battell is hung out, And ſomething to be done immediately.
speeches.Caſſi ▪: 〈◊〉 faſt Titinius, we muſt out and talke.
speeches.〈◊〉: No Caeſar, we will anſwer on their Charge. Make forth, the Generals would haue ſome words.
O Caſſius, Brutus gaue the word too early, Who hauing ſome aduantage on Octauius, Tooke it too eagerly: his Soldiers fell to ſpoyle, Whil'ſt we by Antony are all inclos'd. Theſe tydings will well comfort Caſſius. All diſconſolate, With Pindarus his Bondman, on this Hill. He lies not like the Liuing. O my heart! No, this was he Meſſala, But Caſſius is no more. O ſetting Sunne: As in thy red Rayes thou doeſt ſinke to night; So in his red blood Caſsius day is ſet. The Sunne of Rome is ſet. Our day is gone, Clowds, Dewes, and Dangers come; our deeds are done: Miſtruſt of my ſucceſſe hath done this deed.
Fly further off my Lord: flye further off, Mark Antony is in your Tents my Lord: Flye therefore Noble Caſſius, flye farre off. Aboue. O my Lord. Titinius is encloſed round about With Horſemen, that make to him on the Spurre, Yet he ſpurres on. Now they are almoſt on him: Now Titinius. Now ſome light: O he lights too. Hee's tane. And hearke, they ſhout for ioy.
They are, my Lord. I will be heere againe, euen with a thought. What Pindarus ? Where art thou Pindarus ? Hye you Meſſala, And I will ſeeke for Pindarus the while: Why did'ſt thou ſend me forth braue Caſsius ? Did I not meet thy Friends, and did not they Put on my Browes this wreath of Victorie, And bid me giue it thee? Did'ſt thou not heare their ſhowts? Alas, thou haſt miſconſtrued euery thing. But hold thee, take this Garland on thy Brow, Thy Brutus bid me giue it thee, and I Will do his bidding. Brutus, come apace, And ſee how I regarded Caius Caſsius : By your leaue Gods: This is a Romans part, Come Caſsius Sword, and finde Titinius hart.
He is ſlaine. Braue Titinius, Looke where he haue not crown'd dead Caſsius. What Baſtard doth not? Who will go with me? I will proclaime my name about the Field. I am the Sonne of Marcus Cato, hoe. A Foe to Tyrants, and my Countries Friend. I am the Sonne of Marcus Cato, hoe. And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I, Brutus my Countries Friend: Know me for Brutus.
Yeeld, or thou dyeſt. We muſt not: a Noble Priſoner.
Roome hoe: tell Antony, Brutus is tane.
Ile tell thee newes. Heere comes the Generall, Brutus is tane, Brutus is tane my Lord.
Statillius ſhew'd the Torch-light, but my Lord He came not backe: he is or tane, or ſlaine. What I, my Lord? No, not for all the World. Ile rather kill my ſelfe. O Dardanius. What ill requeſt did Brutus make to thee? Now is that Noble Veſſell full of griefe, That it runnes ouer euen at his eyes.
Shall I doe ſuch a deed? O Clitus. To kill him, Clitus: looke he meditates.
That's not an Office for a friend, my Lord.
Fly, flye my Lord, there is no tarrying heere. Fly my Lord, flye.
Giue me your hand firſt. Fare you wel my Lord. Free from the Bondage you are in Meſſala, The Conquerors can but make a fire of him: For Brutus onely ouercame himſelfe, And no man elſe hath Honor by his death. I, if Meſſala will preferre me to you. I held the Sword, and he did run on it.
